results.title: Nebius raises GPU list prices up to 21% while H100 spot sits at $0.79 - CTOL Digital Solutions
highlights:
Posted prices for four Nebius GPU types rose 17 to 21 percent on 1 October. Its own spot board shows Blackwell chips near 60 percent of list and an H100 at the floor, so the squeeze sits in particular chips and regions.

Nebius told CNBC this week that AI computing prices are rising faster than it expected. On 1 October it lifted the posted price of four GPU types by 17 to 21 percent. Anyone renting GPUs has to decide whether that posted price is what they will pay.

The posted price mostly is not what buyers pay. It rose, but the price at which capacity actually clears is uneven, and Nebius now publishes it. Scarcity is specific to Blackwell chips and some regions, while older H100 capacity is sitting idle.

### What changed in the price list

The Nebius pricing documentation dates two changes. The first took effect on 1 October, when on demand prices per GPU hour rose for four chips. Reuters reported on 17 September that Nebius had announced it, its second price rise in three months.

- B300 went from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21.0 percent, the largest rise.
- B200 went from $7.15 to $8.50, up 18.9 percent.
- H200 went from $4.50 to $5.40, up 20.0 percent.
- H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9 percent, the smallest rise of the four.

The RTX PRO 6000 stayed at $1.80, so the rise did not reach every GPU.

The second change came on 8 October. The preemptible tier, which rents interruptible capacity at a discount, stopped using fixed prices. It moved to dynamic spot pricing that can change every 15 minutes.

One rule in the documentation matters most. The highest spot price is always one cent below the current on demand rate, so the new list price is a ceiling. The floor is $0.79 or $0.99 depending on the chip. The posted price rise matters to a spot buyer only when the market pushes against that ceiling.

...

A reserved H200 rate should be compared with $5.40 on demand at Nebius, $4.29 at Crusoe and a live spot range of $2.00 to $5.09.

...

A run that needs Blackwell in a given week should expect to pay 52 to 62 percent of list.

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Rental Prices Twice in 2026. Nebius Just Did It Again. — AIntOps
highlights:
AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block pricing for GPU instances roughly 15% in January 2026 and another 20% in July. Nebius raised its on-demand GPU prices again on October 1 — the second increase in three months, with some memory pricing up about 41%. Neither company frames these as one-time corrections. They read as a new baseline: the rental price of a GPU is no longer a number you can assume holds from one quarter to the next.

Published October 19, 2026 · 7 min read

## AWS: two hikes, one product line

AWS's EC2 Capacity Block pricing for ML instances moved twice this year. The first increase, reported to take effect around January 4-6, raised rates on the P5 family by roughly 15% — p5e.48xlarge went from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour, and p5en.48xlarge from $36.18 to $41.61. Asked about the change, an AWS spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics it reflects "the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter." The second increase landed July 1, roughly 20%, across the P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de families — one report lists the P6-B300 now billing at $14.04 per accelerator-hour. Both changes applied specifically to Capacity Block reservations, not general on-demand EC2 pricing.

## Nebius: the same pattern, a shorter interval

Nebius notified customers on September 17 that on-demand AI cloud prices would rise again starting October 1 — its second increase in roughly three months. The headline move: H100 GPU-hour pricing went from $3.85 to $4.50, about 17%, with some memory pricing up roughly 41%. The company's own framing points to tight capacity, the same pressure AWS cited.

...

This is our reading, not something either company states directly: a price increase on a GPU rental line reads like an infrastructure cost, not an AI cost, in most reporting structures — it shows up in a cloud bill, under compute, often in a different review than the one that tracks OpenAI or Anthropic API spend. If your AI workload runs partly on rented GPU capacity and partly on provider APIs, the two cost lines move independently and get reviewed by different people, on different schedules, even though both are the same underlying pressure: AI demand outpacing supply.

...

Neither AWS nor Nebius has signaled this is the last increase. Two rounds in a year, from two unrelated providers, each citing supply and demand rather than a one-off event, is a pattern worth budgeting for rather than treating as an anomaly to absorb once and move past.

results.title: Nebius says AI computing prices are rising despite neocloud debt fears
results.author: Arjun Kharpal
highlights:
Nebius is among a new wave of Neocloud companies that are investing billions to buy up Nvidia Add To Watchlist 's graphics processing units, build data centers and rent that capacity.

Nebius ran an auction for computing capacity on Tuesday, which showed continued price rises, the revenue chief said. "We're seeing continued upward mobility in terms of the kind of price per megawatt," he told CNBC.

Price per megawatt, a key measure among new cloud companies, shows how much a company can charge customers for a certain amount of computing capacity.

Chase Lochmiller, CEO of Crusoe, an Nvidia-backed AI company that is building data centers, was also bullish on pricing, saying the company was seeing rising prices for GPUs, including older Nvidia chips.

"We're seeing higher pricing today for A100s than we saw in 2020 or 2021. We're seeing higher pricing for H100s than what we saw when they were first deployed in 2023," Lochmiller said.

"There's tremendous demand and a lot of it is because the underlying model capabilities have gotten so much more advanced that people are just creating so much more value out of the compute infrastructure."

...

The ability to continue renting out older chips at attractive prices is crucial to AI infrastructure companies that need to recover their investments and generate profits, while spending billions on GPUs.

Lochmiller's comments suggest that, at least for Crusoe, older generations of Nvidia chips are commanding higher rental prices than when they were first deployed, potentially strengthening the economics of its AI cloud business.

...

Nebius stock rose on Wednesday after SpaceX Add To Watchlist reported revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range," underscoring the pricing power for those renting out compute capacity.

results.title: Nebius Defends 'Neocloud' Model as AI Compute Prices Climb — TechNewsReel
results.author: TechNewsReel Newsroom
highlights:
Nebius executives are pushing back against investor skepticism regarding the "neocloud" business model, arguing that relentless demand for AI compute is driving prices higher. The company is positioning itself as a stable alternative to competitors facing mounting borrowing costs.

Nebius reports continued upward mobility in price per megawatt, a trend supported by a recent capacity auction. The company has already implemented two price hikes in three months, with rates for selected Nvidia GPUs increasing by 17% to 21% starting October 1. This pricing power is reflected in the company's financials; Nebius reported Q2 revenue of $582.3 million, a 454% increase year-over-year.

...

Neoclouds are specialized AI infrastructure providers that purchase massive quantities of GPUs, primarily from Nvidia, to rent them out for the matrix calculations required for LLM training and inference. Unlike general-purpose cloud providers, these firms optimize specifically for AI workloads. However, the model is extremely capital-intensive, leaving providers highly sensitive to interest rate hikes and the cost of debt financing.

results.title: Is GPU compute tight? The answer is in contract length | SecondSource
highlights:
Correction, November 4, 2026. The version first published on October 18 put a term premium in its headline and conclusion as the shape of the tightness, reading the whole 2.5-to-4-times gap between short and long contracts as tightness, and said CoreWeave's listed prices "have not moved"; those lines were corrected in place on October 18 and October 23. The conclusion is unchanged: GPU compute is tight, but the gap can only be called high, and how much tighter than in past years cannot be said.

...

## Key takeaways

CoreWeave, a cloud company that specializes in renting out GPUs, the chips AI runs on, says rental prices rose about 25% starting in July. Yet a public index that the website getdeploying compiles from the list prices on dozens of providers' websites read only a 5% rise over a year in mid-September. Both numbers can be right. Almost all of CoreWeave's revenue comes from customers on contracts, while the index collects only the hourly, stop-any-time prices listed on websites (pay-as-you-go), so the two numbers measure different prices. Where compute is visibly tight, with more would-be renters than machines, is contract length: customers who sign for only three to six months pay 2.5 to 4 times the price of a five-to-six-year contract. That is above the gap of about 2 times between renting by the hour and signing for three years in the public market (SecondSource's conversion), but the two multiples cover different terms, so the gap can only be called high. No multiple calculated the same way exists for earlier years, so how much tighter than in past years cannot be said. Long contracts also require 20% to 30% up front. In October, after another provider raised list prices, the index's one-year rise reached 18%. CoreWeave's third-quarter results will show how fast new prices lift the average price across all of CoreWeave's contracts.

...

CoreWeave's second-quarter 10-Q says 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts and only about 2% from pay-as-you-go. CoreWeave's pricing page lists the H100, one of NVIDIA's GPU models, at US$6.16 per GPU per hour, the figure read on October 18. The site keeps no older versions, so whether this price moved around July can't be checked. In the public index, CoreWeave also appears at US$6.16.

So the 25% most likely went into the prices of new and renewed contracts: even if the listed price did move, the change would touch only about 2% of revenue. The CFO did not say which kind of price the 25% refers to; this reading rests on the 10-Q and the pricing page. The two numbers also cover different periods, so the two cannot be compared directly: the 25% is one company's single price change in July, and the 5% is a year's rise in dozens of providers' listed prices.

...

## Six: In October, another company's listed prices moved

For the week of October 12, getdeploying's reading became 9% over four weeks and 18% over a year; SecondSource's recomputation from getdeploying's public weekly data matches. In the same period Nebius, another GPU rental company, raised listed prices from October 1 (Nebius pricing page). The H100 went from US$3.85 to US$4.50 an hour, and the increases across the H100 and three other NVIDIA GPU models, the H200, B200 and B300, ranged from 17% to 21%.

So the public index can see price increases; what the index sees are increases in listed prices. The index is calculated by GPU model, and in the week of October 12, 21 of 26 models rose; getdeploying hasn't broken out which providers changed prices or how much each contributed.

...

| Contract | Price, autumn 2026 | Term, and whether the customer can leave early | Source of the figure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pay-as-you-go listed | H100 median US$3.51 an hour (40 providers); specialist GPU clouds US$4.50; big clouds such as Amazon, Microsoft and Google US$7.89; Silicon Data's specialist-cloud H100 rental index US$2.82 on October 17, +6.4% over seven days | Stop at any time | Third-party compilation of listed prices |
| One-year contract | H100 US$1.70 → US$2.35 an hour (October 2025 to March 2026) | One year | Silicon Data figures cited by SemiAnalysis |
| Three-to-six-month contract | CoreWeave about US$40 million per MW per year, about US$7.6 to US$8.4 per GPU per hour | Three to six months | Company-reported |
| Cancellable big order | Google pays SpaceX US$920 million a month to rent 110,000 GB200s, about US$11.6 per GPU per hour, about US$55 million to US$60 million per MW per year | Three years on paper, cancellable on 90 days' notice | Four outlets report the same figures; unit price estimated by SecondSource |
| Five-to-six-year contract | IREN–NVIDIA about US$11.3 million; IREN–Microsoft about US$9.7 million; Nebius–Microsoft at least US$11.6 million; OpenAI–Oracle about US$13.3 million; Nscale–Anthropic about US$16 million (six years); all per MW per year | Five to six years, 20% to 30% prepaid | Press releases, filings and reporting; calculated by SecondSource |
| CoreWeave company-wide average | About US$6.9 million to US$8.2 million per MW per year | All contracts | SecondSource's rough calculation |

...

Details of the public index. Each week getdeploying records every provider's pay-as-you-go listed price. getdeploying takes a median for each provider and then a median across providers, one vote per provider, leaving out reserved and spot prices. SecondSource recomputed October 12 against September 14 from getdeploying's public weekly data: the median change across the 26 models is 8.6%, and against October 13, 2025 it is 18.2%. Nebius's new prices from October 1 were reported by the press by September 17 (Investing.com): the H100 from US$3.85 to US$4.50, the H200 from US$4.50 to US$5.40, the B200 from US$7.15 to US$8.50 and the B300 from US$7.85 to US$9.50. Several outlets called it the second increase in three months. All five data-center models in the index rose between September 14 and October 12: the H100 from US$3.34 to US$3.51, the H200 from US$4.44 to US$4.86, the B200 from US$6.52 to US$7.99, the B300 from US$7.87 to US$8.99 and the A100 from US$1.75 to US$1.82. The rise is uneven across generations: the H100 is up 5% over four weeks, the B200 up 23%. Compute Desk, another index provider, builds its index from completed transactions. Compute Desk says the B300 pay-as-you-go price rose 17 days in a row to a record on October 15, at about US$7 to US$10 an hour, about 64% above November 2025. That account comes from a single secondhand source. The September 18 call also said that a near-double-digit quarterly rise in the public index in the fourth quarter would mean the two measures had converged. A 9% rise over four weeks is already close, but what rose is the listed price itself.

...

Other readings to watch. (1) getdeploying's four-week readings for November and December, and whether Nebius raises prices a third time. If the four-week reading falls back below 3% with no new list-price change, the reading that the public index moves only when sellers change list prices is supported. If the index keeps rising close to double digits a month, and the rise comes from most providers, prices are rising across the board. (2) If Silicon Data's term prices flip so that longer locks cost more, the reading that the market expects spot to fall no longer holds. (3) Any GPU rental company disclosing the share of short contracts among new signings. The September 18 call said the premium sits in "a small slice"; how small, no one has made public. (4) New undelivered contract value, which the industry calls backlog, divided by new contracted power. Backlog rose to US$104.2 billion in the second quarter and added another US$25 billion early in the third, while contracted power rose from 3.7 GW to 4.2 GW. Without the contract years, this ratio can't be turned into an annual figure, so only its direction can be read.

results.title: Andreessen Horowitz reports GPU rental prices rose across every Nvidia chip generation in 2026 · Advance Intelligence
highlights:
In its October 23 Charts of the Week column by Moses Sternstein, Andreessen Horowitz published data from Ornn Data showing that on demand GPU rental rates have risen across every tracked Nvidia generation between January 1, 2026 and October 19, 2026. Using a trailing seven day average indexed to 100 at the start of the year, Ornn's index shows Nvidia H200 rental prices up approximately 160 percent year to date, B200 rates up roughly 120 percent, RTX PRO 6000 Workstation rates up 65 percent, and H100 SXM rates up 35 percent.

Even the six year old Nvidia A100 SXM4, first released in 2020, ended mid October renting for roughly 5 percent more than it did on January 1 after spiking in June. In the accompanying newsletter analysis, a16z noted that comparing historical rental prices against a standard six year straight line depreciation curve yields a 9 percent to 143 percent pricing surplus across the five models, with the sharpest upward inflection beginning in April 2026 alongside surging token volume on platforms like OpenRouter.

Ornn Exchange separately reported ... Because Ornn's index measures spot and short term transacted rates rather than multi year fixed price hyperscaler commitments, the surge primarily reflects acute scarcity for flexible capacity as enterprises and AI labs scale inference and agentic workloads.

results.title: GPUs Are Scarce; for Some, the Money Is Scarcer — Daily Cortex
highlights:
Current rental prices offer a different signal. Renting an Nvidia H100 cost a median $3.70 an hour in the week of Oct. 19, up from $2.98 a year earlier, by GetDeploying’s count of cloud list prices. The makers of chips and chipmaking tools say capacity is their limit. Harder to find may be long-term money to build more, priced very differently for a hyperscaler than for a heavily indebted neocloud.

...

By GetDeploying’s count the H100 rented for a median $3.70 an hour across 40 providers in the week of Oct. 19, against $2.98 across 36 providers in the week of Oct. 20, 2025, up 24 percent in 12 months. The H200 cost $5.00, against $3.50, and the B200 $7.99, against $5.59, each up about 43 percent. Across the 21 models priced at both ends of the year, on-demand prices rose a median 18 percent; 17 rose and four fell. How the Index Works GetDeploying counts price per GPU per hour: an eight-GPU H100 machine renting at $40 an hour counts as $5.00. It takes each provider’s own median first, then the median across providers, and leaves out spot and reserved prices and any model listed by fewer than four providers that week.

...

A second gauge agrees. Ornn’s Compute Price Index, a volume-weighted average of rentals actually transacted, settled on Wednesday at $3.09 an hour for an H100 SXM, up 10.75 percent in a month; its B200 rose 21.92 percent, to $9.40.

...

Tight supply, then, favors those who own capacity and can borrow cheaply; the hyperscalers also charge more for the same chip. The Markup For an H100, GetDeploying finds that AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud charge a median $7.89 an hour on demand, about 75 percent more than dedicated GPU clouds’ $4.50. Rising rents may help the neoclouds too, but their financing risk differs: Nebius’s Mr. Boroditsky told CNBC that it was not in CoreWeave’s position because “we’re not carrying the kind of debt that they are.”

results.title: CoreWeave Bond Yields Hit 15% as AI Funding Fears Rattle Chip Stocks - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Yoon Kyoung-hwan
highlights: NEW YORK — Global equity markets have been sliding with little resistance on concern that debt-funded investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure could buckle under high inflation and high interest rates. Anxiety has spread across markets in particular as the credit standing of CoreWeave, which leases data center space and rents out the AI cloud and computing resources installed inside to Big Tech companies, has deteriorated sharply. With price increases showing no sign of easing and keeping upward pressure on rates, the view is gaining ground that funding costs for AI infrastructure investment could snowball. If Big Tech's AI infrastructure construction projects fail to proceed as planned, the entire AI ecosystem would inevitably take a chain hit, from Nvidia, which supplies graphics processing units to those firms, to the memory chipmakers that provide high-bandwidth memory to chip designers. Beyond that, the U.S. economy, which relies on AI-related investment for a substantial share of its growth, could face a slowdown. With AI-linked stocks enduring an unprecedented slump, Wall Street is split between reading the moves as a precursor to a break in the so-called semiconductor supercycle and dismissing them as excessive worry.

results.title: GPU Cloud Prices October 2026: H100, A100, L40S Across 16 Providers
results.author: Bo Shen
highlights:
# GPU rental prices, early October 2026: list prices barely moved, but where you rent changes the price up to 4.7×

We collected on-demand GPU list prices from 16 cloud providers three times a day from October 7 to 19, 2026. List prices barely moved: 14 of 407 tracked offers changed. The spread between providers is the real story: H100 from $2.99 to $13.98 per GPU-hour (4.7×), A100 2.6×, L40S 2.1×. And 13 of 22 H100 listings didn't say whether the card is SXM, PCIe or NVL, a difference worth 2.25× in served tokens in our tests.

...

Since October 7 we've collected on-demand GPU list prices three times a day: 42 snapshots so far, about 370 offers from 16 providers. Sources: the Lambda, DigitalOcean and Vultr APIs, and NVIDIA Brev's public catalog, which covers AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud, Nebius, Crusoe, Hyperstack, Massed Compute and others. The live table is on our GPU prices page. This is the first look at what twelve days of it show; the full October index follows on November 1.

## List prices barely moved

Of 407 offers we tracked across the period, 14 changed price at all:

- One real on-demand cut: an 8×A100 offer from Excess Supply dropped from $3.60 to $1.62 per GPU-hour on October 10 (−55%).
- Back and forth: Google Cloud's 8×H100 alternated between $12.41 and $13.98 per GPU-hour, and its T4 offers moved by about 1%. This looks like the catalog reporting different regions on different days rather than price changes.
- Spot prices moved more: DigitalOcean's spot price for AMD MI355X rose from $2.97 to $5.50 per GPU-hour (+85%), MI350X from $2.46 to $3.50 (+42%), and NVIDIA B300 fell from $8.00 to $6.17 (−23%).

On-demand list prices behave like price lists, not markets: they change in steps, rarely. Whatever is moving in GPU pricing week to week (availability, spot and marketplace prices, negotiated discounts) doesn't show up in the list.

## Where you rent matters far more

The same GPU model costs very different amounts depending on the provider. Taking each provider's cheapest on-demand offer per GPU-hour on October 19:

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest | Median | Most expensive | Spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 11 | $2.99 (Vultr) | $3.56 | $13.98 (Google Cloud) | 4.7× |
| A100 | 10 | $1.62 (Hyperstack, Massed Compute, Excess Supply) | $1.98 | $4.18 (Google Cloud) | 2.6× |
| L40S | 9 | $1.06 (Massed Compute) | $1.86 | $2.23 (AWS) | 2.1× |
| H200 | 3 | $4.47 (DigitalOcean) | $4.80 | $6.48 (Nebius) | 1.4× |
| AMD MI300X | 2 | $2.59 (DigitalOcean) | $3.29 | $3.99 (Vultr) | 1.5× |

The big clouds sit at the top of each range. Most of the market clusters well below them: eight of eleven H100 providers list between $2.99 and $4.41.

...

These are list prices at collection time for on-demand capacity. They exclude storage, egress, reserved and committed-use discounts, and they don't tell you whether capacity is available: most offers in the catalog carry no availability flag. Brev's catalog reports one region per offer, which can change between snapshots. Twelve days is a short window. RunPod and peer-to-peer marketplaces where hosts set their own prices aren't included.
